The specifics though

Mid sides converter I think you meant? - Its a little virtual piece of equipment that takes an LR input and output a Mid and a Sides. You can then manipulate those audio streams separately. It's a trick using phase, but the result is that you can have things that sound like they're panned in left and right but somehow not in the middle or vice versa. Or you can use it lightly to give things presence etc.

Channel interfaces - Audio interfaces convert analog audio signal into digital signal for recording into a DAW. It has 2 inputs hence the 2 channels.

I mean, yeah, this is great. But the Internet is by design a "dumb" network with the smarts "on the edges", as opposed to the old phone system. This means you have different systems and devices sending packets to each other. Any time two different systems can talk to each other you have the potential for one to cause the other harm, intentionally or not. And while this article presents an interesting history of l0pht and that famous Congressional testimony, the fact is there is not really a way to fix this problem without fundamentally changing the nature of the Internet. And before someone suggests that a centralized network would be better, remember that it was certainly possible to hack the Bell system, and that viruses spread just fine in the days before everybody was on the Internet.

I live in a relatively high-crime area and am out a lot, so I built a home alarm system. A 433mhz receiver and some magnetic door sensors from Ebay, then used the code from NinjaBlocks (with some edits) to intercept signals, which then calls different shell scripts depending on the state of the alarm (safe, armed, locked-down) which is set by another 433mhz fob. I put it in a box with a little UPS, a small amplifier, and 2x 3" speakers, and it even runs for 2 hours if the power is cut. Any door, window, or other trigger sends me a text message as long as I remember to set it to "away" state.

Further additions will include some motion-sensing and 2 more Pis spaced in a triangle, which should let me triangulate and monitor moving objects broadcasting short-range 433mhz, such as dog collars. I also have a transmitter on the Pi which isn't currently being used, but will eventually trigger dumb devices (lights, cameras, etc) powering up as needed through cheap 433mhz plugs.

I'm working on a temperature-controller using Pis mounted just outside each room's air vent, which use L298N motor drivers to open/close the vents based on both trend data and basic motion sensors in the room. The simple notion is that my air conditioner doesn't need to deliver cooling to the bedroom all day long while I'm in the office, and a few hundred $$ of management now could save me that much per month going forward. The further I get into this project, however, the more likely I am to centralize the management to a hand-built motorized duct divider in the attic instead of per-room robotics, which are turning out to be more expensive than they should be.

I have another half dozen projects scattered here and there as well. One half-finished project is a voice interface for...well, everything, the end result hopefully being every light and device in the house able to be toggled over 433mhz. Another has 3x Pis spread across my front-facing windows that snap motion-sensor images of anyone who gets close. Of course my whole media setup is run with Pi heads which share a SQL database and 30Tb of storage on a Linux server in the closet.

Some friends and I are trying to build a wifi mesh network of outdoor game cams, with the hope being that ranchers/hunters can simply drive by the cameras and the latest images will upload to their laptops/phones. Battery packs and moisture are making this one tougher than it should be though.
This is always something I've wanted to do. How long did it take you, and how hard would you say it was?

It wasn't as easy as I expected, but the biggest difficulty was the parts. I went through several cheap 433 receivers before finally finding one that would get signals from the other end of my house consistently. This is very similar to what I landed on:

http://www.ebay.com/itm/433Mhz-Superheterodyne-3400RF-Transmitter-and-Receiver-Kit-For-Arduino-ARM-MCU-/121597448874

...with a shitton of these:

http://www.ebay.com/itm/Wireless-Door-Window-Gap-Sensor-Dector-433MHz-4pcs-With-Antenna-4-pcs-per-Lot-/291443534248

The second big sticking point was the conversion from simply reading signals out of the air - a feat easily accomplished with NinjaBlocks' 433Utils (https://github.com/ninjablocks/433Utils) - to automating based on what was read. NB's code doesn't output in a format that can be written from stdout to a file or a variable, so it's not so simple as just capturing incoming signals from their existing binary (no "./RFSniffer > watchfile.out" for us!). I'm not a C programmer, so I had to do a LOT of whacking at this part, and know it could be done much more elegantly. With my limited skills I simply modified the 433Utils RFSniffer.cpp to directly call the shell script itself and hard-coded/compiled the individual signal codes into the sniffer end, meaning every time I add a new sensor I also have to recompile my sniffer (ugh):

 if (mySwitch.getReceivedValue() == 5592405 ) {
 system("sudo sh /home/pi/sec/scripts/sec.sh front_door");
 }
 if (mySwitch.getReceivedValue() == 1398101 ) {
 system("sudo sh /home/pi/sec/scripts/sec.sh garage_door");
 }
 if (mySwitch.getReceivedValue() == 15279465 ) {
 system("sudo sh /home/pi/sec/scripts/sec.sh back_door");
 }

The sec.sh script checks a flat file for the alarm state (0, 1, or 2) and executes based on the incoming $1 variable (back_door, garage_door, etc) and the state. The flat files ensure that the system boots back to the previous state (even if it was blaring), and a simple 1-minute cron check ensures that the sniffer is always running.

I pulled my voices from an AT&T site (http://www2.research.att.com/~ttsweb/tts/demo.php), and can switch between several male or female notifications on the fly. In "safe" mode opening any door/window results in a loud "ding" followed by a voice succinctly stating the door/window that was opened.

I built the existing system over about a month of semi-dedicated work, but still have a considerable amount to do to it. Right now it'll alert/text me when things open, but the actual alarm sounding is a bit wonky, and getting it to shut off sometimes takes a few tries since it has to receive/cache a "code" from a 433mhz wall panel and the Pi stays pretty much CPU-pegged all day long. I'll be upgrading the board to a Pi2 this summer, and expect it to perform a lot better.

I have one in my tortoise's house. It does many things. I use it to control the ambient temperature in her house and her greenhouse. I use IFTTT to pull weather data to trigger a heat lamp in her greenhouse if the UV index drops below a certain point. I find the current low priced home automation products such as remote outlets and sensors to be very unreliable. I use it to control lights locally through my network rather than through a crappy cloud service. It also runs a web server that allows me to make changes to any of the triggers I have set. I have an cheap IR camera attached that aids in motion sensing and it works as a webcam. I have an arduino connected to it, with a servo motor glued to a dial on her heat pad to adjust according to changes in the ambient temperature. I have temperature and vibration sensors to detect her movement. If she leaves her house, her UV light turns off. If she is present in her house, her greenhouse heat lamp stays off. As time goes on, I add more and more stuff. I could go on for a while longer but I think you get the picture. It's a little overkill but it's been great for learning scripting, etc.
